thread: Follow a coin from the tools that strike its design into the many forms money takes in people's hands, then into a museum cabinet where its images and history can be rediscovered. The swarm meets engraved dies, curious tokens, animal emblems and tiny portraits along the way.

candidates.name: Berlin Münzkabinett
candidates.why: A coin cabinet with thousands of minting tools and dies, alongside coins, medals and casts: a workshop full of little stamps and the shapes they leave behind.

candidates.name: Bank of Canada Museum
candidates.why: Its currency collection and online exhibits bring together coins, tokens, banknotes and unconventional forms of money, with stories about how they were made and used.

candidates.name: Numismatic Museum of Athens
candidates.why: Ancient and later coins share the collection with seals, weights and medals; miniature animals, gods and geometric marks can emerge from the museum's exhibitions.

candidates.name: American Numismatic Association Money Museum
candidates.why: Virtual exhibitions and collection stories trace coins, tokens and other money across places and periods, with a mini mint and unusual coin designs to explore.

candidates.name: Currency Museum, Bank of Japan
candidates.why: Japanese currency ranges from large oval gold pieces to small copper coins and early notes, with exhibits and guides that connect their forms to everyday use.

candidates.name: Museums Victoria
candidates.why: Its collections include Australian coins, trade tokens and banknotes, giving the swarm stamped creatures and objects from the places where money circulated.

candidates.name: The Fitzwilliam Museum
candidates.why: The museum's coins and medals sit among a broad collection of art and historical objects, offering miniature designs and the larger visual worlds around them.

candidates.name: Heberden Coin Room
candidates.why: Oxford's coin collection spans Greek, Roman, Celtic, Byzantine, Islamic and Chinese money, a cabinet of tiny portraits, symbols and changing shapes.
